rubrics.title: Imperial College London undergraduate marking scale and degree classification (College-wide)
rubrics.body:
MARK SCALE
Every assessment component is marked on a 0-100 scale (recorded to two decimal places). Module pass mark: 40 at Levels 4-6 (Years 1-3 of BSc/BEng/MSci/MEng); 50 at Level 7 (final year of MSci/MEng). A marginal fail (30.00-39.99 at Levels 4-6; 40.00-49.99 at Level 7) may be compensated at the Board of Examiners' discretion. Reassessed modules are capped at the pass mark.

CLASS BANDS (Bachelor's and integrated Master's honours, on the weighted average)
70 and above: First Class
60-69: Upper Second (2:1)
50-59: Lower Second (2:2)
40-49: Third
Below 40 (below 50 at Level 7): Fail
From 2025-26 the regulations state that weighted averages are not rounded; candidates just below a boundary are instead considered under each Board of Examiners' approved borderline criteria, and the reasons for any uplift (or not) are recorded.

HOW MARKING MUST BE DONE
The College requires marking to be fair, objective and transparent and carried out against defined marking criteria; markers should be given the marking criteria and a model answer for every assessment. Written examinations are marked anonymously. Work counting towards classification is second marked (blind double marking or first marking plus check marking); final-year major projects are always blind double marked. Where two markers differ by 5 marks or less the average may be taken; larger differences are resolved by discussion or a third marker. Samples (top, middle, bottom, all fails and all work within about 2.5 marks of a class boundary) go to an External Examiner.

USING THIS RUBRIC
Imperial does not publish a single College-wide set of qualitative grade descriptors: what a First or a 2:1 answer looks like is defined by each department's own criteria and the module's model answer. When no departmental criteria are available, mark against the question's model answer / mark scheme and convert to a percentage that maps onto the bands above. Expected depth rises with level: the FHEQ descriptors in the regulations describe Level 7 learning as mastery of a complex and specialised area of knowledge and skills.
rubrics.source_note: Regulations for Taught Programmes of Study 2024-25 v1.0: paras 133-134 and 142 (marking scale, pass marks, compensation, p.29-30), paras 168-191 (marking and moderation, p.33-36), paras 209-214 (classification bands, borderline, Table 9 year weightings, p.39+), Table 4 (FHEQ level descriptors, p.22-23). Rounding removal from 'Changes to Academic Regulations 2025.26 Taught' (para 226 now 230): https://www.imperial.ac.uk/media/imperial-college/administration-and-support-services/registry/academic-governance/public/regulations/2025-26/Changes-to-Academic-Regulations-2025.26-Taught.pdf; the 2026-27 changes document lists no change to pass marks or boundaries. Marking practice also from 'Protocol for marking and moderation' v2.2, Oct 2023, s.2.1-2.6. The 2026-27 Regulations for Taught Programmes PDF exists but could not be fetched.

rubrics.title: Bioengineering undergraduate individual project and report marking criteria
rubrics.body:
Bioengineering publishes band descriptors for its final-year individual project. The written report criteria below are the department's standard for any substantial scientific/engineering report. (Project weighting: planning report 10%, oral presentation 20%, final report 70%, of which the written element is 80% and supervisor-assessed professional conduct 20%. Reports over the word limit are unlikely to score above 59%.)

WRITTEN REPORT BANDS
A* 90-100 (high First): exemplary, close to publishable. Professional-standard, complex evaluation of a broad literature; meticulous, systematic data recording; data and terminology at journal/industry standard; complex, accurate, well-justified interpretations; highly innovative, in-depth discussion that confirms or challenges existing models with outstanding synthesis and critique; thorough grasp of wider context; excellent independent problem-solving; concise, logical, fully compliant writing with broad, journal-style referencing; original, publication-quality figures.
A+ 80-89 (mid First): excellent, publishable after some editing; very careful evaluation, very good attention to detail, some innovation in the discussion, good grasp of context, very highly developed problem-solving.
A 70-79 (low First): very good, publishable only with significant editing; careful evaluation and sound literature knowledge; complex, justified interpretations; well-considered, in-depth discussion; sound grasp of context; some independent interpretation; logically structured and correctly referenced; figures partly original and of very good quality.
B 60-69 (Upper Second): good. Few observations are complex; data accurate but needing more attention to detail; terminology mostly accurate; some complex interpretations, well justified; discussion questions models in places and synthesises sources; reasonable grasp of context; some citation gaps or irrelevant citations.
C 50-59 (Lower Second): mostly sound but lacking detail; terminology sometimes wrong; few complex interpretations, some unsupported by data or literature; some independent thought but no real engagement with existing models; limited context; some irrelevant material, structural and grammatical problems, inaccurate references; some irrelevant or poor-quality figures.
D 40-49 (Third): sound only in parts; general observations only; data often insufficiently accurate; terminology often wrong; very general, weakly supported interpretations; inconsistent discussion; poor grasp of context; little problem-solving or independence; confused structure, frequent errors, inadequate citations; many irrelevant figures.
Below 40: fail (the department's other project rubrics define 30-39 as little or no engagement or understanding).
rubrics.source_note: Department of Bioengineering, Undergraduate Individual Project Handbook 2025-26: component weightings pp.5-6; Appendix 2 marking criteria, final report written element pp.23-29 (planning report, ethics, professional conduct and presentation rubrics pp.21-31). Applies to MEng Biomedical Engineering and Molecular Bioengineering final-year projects. No published Bioengineering descriptors for written exams were found; the department's examinations page says only that marking follows 'strict marking guidelines' with first and second marking.

rubrics.title: Imperial Business School undergraduate general marking criteria
rubrics.body:
The Business School's 'General Marking Criteria Undergraduate' apply across assessment types (exam answers, essays and written coursework). Each band is judged on five aspects: overall impression, knowledge of the field's models, ideas, concepts and techniques; critical analysis, independent thought and application; structure and synthesis; and use of sources, academic practice and presentation.

85-100 OUTSTANDING (First): exceptional knowledge, reading well beyond core texts, original and independent thought. Exceptional command of models, concepts and techniques; very strong critical analysis and application; excellent structure and synthesis, clear throughout; wide range of highly relevant sources showing independent research; full adherence to academic practice; sophisticated expression.

70-84 EXCELLENT (First): extensive knowledge and wide reading; evidence of independent thinking and the ability to analyse and apply material; high-level structure with clear arguments; considerable use of relevant sources; professional presentation that follows academic conventions; very good language.

60-69 GOOD (Upper Second): above-average knowledge backed by thorough research; good command of models and concepts; some independent thinking, critical analysis and application; sound structure giving coherent, relevant arguments; good use of sources with minor omissions; referencing mostly correct; clearly written.

50-59 SATISFACTORY (Lower Second): knowledge of the subject but only basic command of models and concepts; critical analysis attempted but poorly or inconsistently executed; little independent thought and limited application; adequate but poorly structured argument with little synthesis; reasonable but incomplete use of sources; competent writing with some errors.

40-49 PASS (Third): limited knowledge and a weak grasp of basic ideas; minimal critical analysis; arguments largely descriptive and inconsistently structured; limited reading with major omissions; limited adherence to good practice; inconsistent or poor language.

0-39 FAIL: very little or no knowledge and a clear lack of comprehension of the main ideas; no independent thought, inadequate analysis and no application; no evidence of an ability to structure an argument; very little reading; disregard for academic practice; inarticulate language.

Pass mark 40%. Students within 2% below a class boundary may be considered for the higher class; this requires more than half of individual assessments in the higher class, no compensated or retaken modules without accepted mitigation, and (where specified) the final project in the higher class.
rubrics.source_note: Imperial Business School, Intercalated BSc (Management) Programme Handbook 2024-25 (v24.10.24), 'Assessment Scheme' section, table 'General Marking Criteria Undergraduate' (pp.21-23) and borderline rules (p.21). Hosted under a Faculty of Medicine web path but the programme is run by the Business School. No handbook for the BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science was publicly available, so these are the School's published UG criteria for the iBSc and may not be identical for other Business School UG programmes.

rubrics.title: Chemistry undergraduate exam marking scheme and research project marking criteria
rubrics.body:
Chemistry publishes how its exams are marked and graded rather than a set of qualitative band descriptors; for what each band demands, combine this with the College-wide scale.

HOW AN EXAM ANSWER IS MARKED
Each question carries a fixed number of marks (typically out of 25) awarded against the question's mark scheme. The paper total is then scaled to a percentage (e.g. a paper of three 25-mark questions, out of 75, is multiplied by 4/3). Every exam question is marked by two examiners: if they differ by one mark or less out of 25 the higher mark is awarded; larger differences are resolved by the markers agreeing a mark. A committee may, rarely, moderate a whole question or paper (e.g. if it proved too hard or too long); any moderation is reviewed by the Examination Board, and no other adjustment is made. If a candidate answers more questions than required, the mark is the average across all questions attempted, so extra answers do not help.

GRADE BANDS (module/paper percentage)
A: 70-100 (First-class standard)
B: 60-69 (Upper Second standard)
C: 50-59 (Lower Second standard)
D: 40-49 (Third-class standard)
F: below 40 (fail)
G: below 25 (bad fail)
Pass mark: 40% in Years 1-3; 50% in Years 4-5 (Master's level). Resits are normally capped at 40% unless extenuating circumstances are accepted.

DEGREE CLASS
Year totals are credit-weighted averages; for the MSci they are combined 6:16:29:29 into a mark out of 1000: 700-1000 First; 600-699 Upper Second; 500-599 Lower Second; 400-499 Third; below 400 fail. Candidates within 20 marks (out of 1000) below a boundary are reviewed by the examiners, including External Examiners, and may be promoted.

RESEARCH PROJECT REPORTS (department project marking protocol)
Independent assessors mark the report out of 100: background and introduction 15, quality of experimental work 30, understanding and analysis 30, presentation and clarity 25. Reference points: ~85 clear First - mastery of the subject, all key references, an outstanding volume of publishable-quality results, lucid and mature analysis, flawless English. 70 (2:1/First border) - aims clear, reliable publishable-quality results, logical problem-solving, essentially error-free. 60 (2:2/2:1 border) - coherent narrative, useful well-documented data with some inconsistencies, reasoned justification of decisions, good English. 50 (Third/2:2 border) - most aims identified, some useful data, attempts at reasoned analysis, acceptable English. 40 (fail/Third border) - aims poorly conveyed, few meaningful results, little critical analysis, hard to follow. ~20 clear fail - no real background, analysis or order.

WHEN MARKING A PRACTICE ANSWER
Mark each question against its mark allocation (out of 25 where applicable), total the marks, scale to a percentage and report the letter band above.

rubrics.title: CLCC / I-Explore and Horizons humanities and social sciences assessment expectations and level descriptors
rubrics.body:
CLCC does not publish a public band-by-band rubric for its Humanities and Social Sciences (HSS) modules; module lecturers issue the specific criteria. What it does publish is below: the class labels it uses, what markers look for, and level descriptors.

CLASS LABELS
Work is assessed against the assignment brief and the College's grading criteria and placed as excellent (First, 70+), very good (2:1, 60-69), good (2:2, 50-59) or adequate (Third, 40-49); below 40 fails. All credit-bearing written work is double marked, with a third marker if the two disagree, and marks are provisional until the external examiner and the June Board of Examiners confirm them.

WHAT MARKERS LOOK FOR IN HSS WRITING
- A critical argument: build a case, evaluate appropriate evidence, and explain why each point matters (critical means careful analysis, not negativity).
- Structure: an introduction stating the purpose and direction of the argument; body paragraphs that each make one distinct point; a conclusion that draws the argument together without new material.
- Style: precise, formal, readable prose using the module's terminology accurately, without cliches.
- Referencing: Harvard by default (or another agreed style used consistently); poor or inconsistent referencing loses marks.
- Length: keep to the word count or time limit; going significantly over or under reduces the mark (word counts include in-text citations, footnotes, tables and captions, not the bibliography).
- Following the brief and module-specific presentation instructions.

LEVEL DESCRIPTORS (expected standard rises with the student's level)
Level 4: knows the core principles, concepts and terms; describes, analyses and interprets defined aspects of a subject; communicates accurately for purpose and audience.
Level 5: critical understanding of principles and techniques; applies knowledge accurately to a range of problems and evaluates using established techniques; communicates arguments and ideas effectively.
Level 6: systematic, partly specialist knowledge informed by current thinking; handles abstract ideas and argues from competing perspectives; defines complex problems, chooses investigative strategies and evaluates their outcomes; communicates complex arguments effectively.
Level 7: deep, systematic understanding of a specialised field linked to other disciplines; works at a high level of abstraction; critically responds to existing theories and methods and proposes new concepts or approaches.

rubrics.title: Design Engineering undergraduate grade scale for exams and coursework
rubrics.body:
Design Engineering marks exams and coursework on a percentage scale linked to a letter grade, a one-word descriptor and an honours class. Detailed criteria for individual pieces of coursework and design projects are set in each module's marking scheme (issued on the module's VLE page) rather than in the handbook; exam answers are judged against the module's intended learning outcomes, which define what students must be able to do.

GRADE SCALE
A* (85 and above): Exceptional - First class.
A range (70-84; sub-grades A-, A, A+ rising through the band): Excellent - First class.
B+ 67-69 / B 63-66 / B- 60-62: Very Good - Upper Second.
C+ 57-59 / C 53-56 / C- 50-52: Good - Lower Second.
D+ 47-49 / D 43-46 / D- 40-42: Good/Pass - Third class.
E+ 37-39 / E 33-36 / E- 30-32: Marginal fail (a failing mark within 10 marks of the pass mark).
F (below 30): Fail.

PASS MARKS AND RULES
Pass mark 40% at FHEQ Levels 4-6 (Years 1-3) and 50% at Level 7 (Year 4), so at Level 7 the marginal-fail zone is 40-49. A module is passed with a 40% weighted average across its assessments (50% at Level 7) plus a pass in any assessment designated 'must pass'. Coursework up to 24 hours late is capped at the pass mark; later than that scores 0. Resits may be capped at the pass mark.

MARKING PROCESS
Major coursework items are double marked, with moderation resolving differences between supervisor and second marker on project reports. External Examiners review exam scripts, individual project reports and group project outcomes. All marks issued during the year are provisional until the Board of Examiners meets in July; the department states that no quota is applied to the proportion of students in each class.

WHEN MARKING A PRACTICE ANSWER
Award marks against the question's own mark scheme, convert to a percentage, and report the letter grade and descriptor from the scale above.
rubrics.source_note: Dyson School of Design Engineering Undergraduate Handbook 2025-26 (v2): Section 5.9 'Grades & Marks for Exams & Coursework' (grade table and footnotes, p.31); Section 5.1 'Passing the year' (p.26); Section 5.5 resits and 5.7 coursework/late submission and double marking (pp.28-29); Section 5.8 learning outcomes; Section 10.5 Board of Examiners (p.51). The sub-grade boundaries within the A band are garbled in the extracted PDF text, so only the A* (85+) and A-range (70-84) limits are given. No qualitative band-by-band descriptors beyond the one-word labels are published.

rubrics.title: Earth Science and Engineering undergraduate marking criteria (Swanson Criteria for written work)
rubrics.body:
ESE marks free-form written coursework (e.g. essays) and the free-form written parts of exams against the Swanson Criteria. Markers weigh: relevance to the question, understanding, synthesis and critical analysis, structure, reading beyond the lectures, independent enquiry or creativity, referencing, and presentation/spelling/grammar. Unless a task says otherwise, referencing, presentation, spelling and grammar together make up 20% of the mark. Other coursework (field reports, lab work, projects) has its own marking scheme. Exam scripts and major coursework are marked by at least two staff against a pre-agreed marking scheme, anonymously by candidate number.

90-100 (First): a thorough grasp of the subject with the ability to synthesise and critique, and evidence of productive reading beyond the lectures. Outstanding work and presentation; substantial independent enquiry, critical thought or creativity; near-perfect recall, reasoning and accuracy; considerable innovation in interpretation and problem-solving, with alternatives assessed or the chosen approach justified.

70-89 (First): the same qualities, but occasionally falling below a uniformly excellent level. Excellent work and presentation.

60-69 (Upper Second): a good grasp of the subject and some ability to synthesise and critique, but short of excellence in one or both. Well organised, clearly presented, logical and sufficiently detailed; thorough grasp of the relevant principles; some independent enquiry or critical thought; competent interpretation and problem-solving with some weighing of alternatives or justification of approach.

50-59 (Lower Second): satisfactory but lacking distinction or with clear lapses. Essential elements of solutions correct; basic understanding of principles; little independent enquiry; arguments reach reasonable but not fully correct conclusions; competent but unimaginative mapping or design work; adequate presentation and consistent effort.

40-49 (Third / Pass): adequate knowledge but poor appreciation of the subject. Sufficient factual recall but limited understanding of principles; some competence in routine tasks; presentation or consistency of effort somewhat lacking.

0-39 (Fail): basically incorrect; defective recall of basic facts and little or no understanding of principles; no workable approach to the desired outcome; unacceptably brief or poorly presented.

Pass mark 40% (50% for Level 7 modules in Years 3-4). Degree class on the weighted aggregate: 70 First, 60 Upper Second, 50 Lower Second, 40 Third; students within 2% of a boundary are considered for the higher class on their overall performance.
rubrics.source_note: Department of Earth Science and Engineering, UG Programme Handbook 2024-25: 'Assessment process' (pp.20-21), 'Swanson Criteria for the assessment of written work' (pp.21-22), 'Examination Procedures' (p.24), 'Year marks and degree classification' (p.26). A 2025-26 ESE UG handbook is linked from the department's Undergraduate resources page (https://www.imperial.ac.uk/engineering/departments/earth-science/current-student-staff-info/ug/) but could not be fetched, so these criteria are from the 2024-25 edition.

rubrics.title: Electrical and Electronic Engineering undergraduate exam marking and grade bands
rubrics.body:
EEE publishes its exam marking procedure and letter-grade bands, not qualitative descriptors per band; detailed mark allocations are in each question's marking scheme.

WHAT EXAMS TEST
EEE exams test numerical problem solving, reasoned explanation of engineering choices, and comparison of the features of different systems. Almost every exam question is worth 100 marks; papers with different numbers of questions are scaled so the paper total becomes a percentage.

HOW A SCRIPT IS MARKED
1. The module's lecturer first-marks each question against the marking scheme.
2. A second marker checks the marks against the scheme, confirms every part of every answer was seen, and checks agreement with the first marker.
3. The two markers meet to agree final marks.
4. External Examiners may inspect papers and marking.
5. A small committee (Examinations Officer, Head of Department, Director of Undergraduate Studies, Senior Tutor) reviews overall marks. The department may moderate a question or paper (e.g. if it was too difficult or too long); any moderation is reported to the Board of Examiners. Where there are unusually many failures or A grades, piecewise-linear scaling that preserves rank order may be applied.

GRADE BANDS
A: 70% and above - First class standard
B: 60-69% - Upper Second (2:1)
C: 50-59% - Lower Second (2:2)
D: 40-49% - Third class
E: below 40% - Fail
Letter grades given during the year (labs, coursework, Year 3 autumn exams) are provisional until moderation and the July Board of Examiners.

COURSEWORK, LABS AND PROJECTS
Coursework using design or simulation software is assessed through written reports. Projects are assessed through oral presentations and written reports covering design, implementation and testing, with evidence of practical, communication and planning skills. Labs may be assessed by computer-based tests, oral exams, formal lab reports or computer-based exercises. For example, the BEng final-year Individual Project (ELEC60017) is 5% interim report, 85% final report, 10% poster presentation, plus a must-pass professional-competencies element; the Year 3 MEng group project is 10% leaflet, 55% presentation and demonstration, 30% report, 5% peer assessment.

WHEN MARKING A PRACTICE ANSWER
Mark each question out of its stated marks against the marking scheme, scale the paper to a percentage and report the letter grade.
rubrics.source_note: EEE online course handbook, Examinations > After your exams > Results (grade bands, marking procedure, scaling, moderation; page last modified 25 Sep 2026). Also: 'Assessment (UG and MSc)' page https://www.imperial.ac.uk/engineering/departments/electrical-engineering/study/current-students-course-handbook/assessment-ug-and-msc/ (what exams test, report/project/lab assessment, piecewise-linear scaling); 'Projects' page (group project weightings); ELEC60017 Individual Project module descriptor (revised Jan 2025). No published band-by-band qualitative descriptors were found for EEE.

rubrics.title: Mathematics undergraduate marking and classification scheme
rubrics.body:
Mathematics marks exams numerically against a per-question mark scheme and then maps raw marks onto the College scale; it does not publish wordy band descriptors in its handbook. Use the bands below with the question's own mark allocation.

EXAM FORMAT (what a paper looks like)
Year 1 10-ECTS modules: 2 hours, four questions. Year 2 core 10-ECTS modules: 3 hours, six questions. 5-ECTS (Years 1-2) and 7.5-ECTS (Year 3) modules: about 1.5 hours, three questions. Year 4 (MSci, Level 7): 2 hours, four questions, the fourth normally a 'mastery' question on extension material studied independently. End-of-year exams are typically 70% of a Year 1 module and 80% in Year 2.

HOW RAW MARKS BECOME PERCENTAGES
For each module the examiners fix four raw-mark boundaries: P (pass/fail), T (2:1/2:2), E (First/2:1) and M (realistic maximum). These are mapped piecewise-linearly to 40, 60, 70 and 100 (0 stays 0); in Year 4 P maps to 50. A Liaison Panel checks boundaries for comparability across modules.

CLASS BANDS
70+: First; 60-69: Upper Second; 50-59: Lower Second; 40-49: Third; below 40 fail (below 50 at Level 7). Pass mark 40% for Years 1-3 (50% for Introduction to University Mathematics) and 50% for Year 4.

BORDERLINES
A First is automatic for a programme total of 69.5 or more. BSc candidates on 68-69.5 are promoted if their Year 3 total is at least 69.5 or they have 30 ECTS of Year 3 maths modules at 70+. MSci candidates on 68-69.5 are promoted if two of: Year 4 total at least 69.5; MSci project at 70+; 22.5 ECTS of Year 4 electives at 70+.

WHEN MARKING A PRACTICE ANSWER
Award marks against the question's own mark allocation, total them, and place the script relative to the P/T/E/M standards above to give the percentage and band. The handbook gives no further qualitative descriptors.
rubrics.source_note: Department of Mathematics Undergraduate Programme Handbook 2026-27: Section 3 'Assessment' (exam formats and weightings, pp.33-41), Section 4 'Marks, Year Totals and Year Weightings' (raw-mark scaling P/T/E/M, p.43; class thresholds, p.44) and 'Criteria for Degree Classification at Borderlines' (pp.44-45); pass marks Section 2 p.18. The handbook states no qualitative grade descriptors; module-level criteria are on the internal Maths TIPS/Blackboard pages.

rubrics.title: School of Medicine marking criteria for exams and essays
rubrics.body:
The criteria list specific marks within each band, and answers are judged against what a 'Very Good' (model) answer would contain. Allowance is made for the year of study and for the time available in an exam. Problem-type answers are marked on a semi-absolute scale.

EXCEPTIONAL (85, 90, 95, 100)
Exceptionally well presented; full command of the concepts and facts; marked critical or analytical ability; originality; substantial reading beyond the taught material where relevant. Goes beyond what is expected at this stage of the degree.

EXCELLENT - approx. First (72, 76, 80)
Very well presented with command of the concepts and facts; shows most of the exceptional features but falls short on one or two of them.

VERY GOOD - approx. Upper Second (62, 65, 68)
Clear grasp of concepts and facts; an accurate account of the taught material, essentially the model answer; some evidence of wider reading or of critical/analytical ability.

GOOD - approx. Lower Second (52, 55, 58)
Grasp of the basic concepts and facts; a mainly accurate account of at least half of the taught material but going no further, or going further but spoiled by significant errors.

ADEQUATE - approx. Third (42, 45, 48)
Moderate grasp; major errors or excessive brevity, but contains at least about a third of what a Very Good answer would, enough to reach degree level.

FAIL (below 40)
35-38: weak grasp, about a third of the Very Good content but with major misunderstandings, or too brief.
30: confused reading of the question; less than a third of the expected relevant knowledge.
25: insufficient relevant knowledge to reach degree level.
15-20: so inaccurate, irrelevant or brief that it shows only vague understanding (under a quarter of the expected content).
5-10: only one to three correct, relevant statements. 0: nothing correct or relevant.

FEEDBACK should comment on structure, referencing and diagrams as well as content and the student's understanding of the topic.
rubrics.source_note: 'MARKING CRITERIA for EXAMS and ESSAYS', single-page staff document hosted on the Faculty of Medicine education site (education.med.imperial.ac.uk/Staff). The document itself is undated and does not name the programme (MBBS or BSc) it applies to, so its currency for 2026-27 is unverified. A related older Faculty of Medicine report/project mark scheme (May 2012, Year 4 BSc surgery path) uses the same band structure: https://education.med.imperial.ac.uk/Years/4-1213/surg/markscheme.pdf

rubrics.title: Physics undergraduate exam marking and moderation scheme
rubrics.body:
Physics publishes how its exams are marked, moderated and scaled, but no band-by-band qualitative descriptors; for those, use the College-wide bands. Questions carry indicative marks for each part, and scripts are marked against the question's marking scheme.

HOW A SCRIPT IS MARKED
Every exam script is marked independently by a first and a second marker, and one of the academics collates the agreed marks. Marks are entered by an administrator and cross-checked by error-checking software against the academic's figures.

MODERATION AND SCALING
The marks printed on the paper are indicative, not definitive. Markers moderate each exam so that the average mark, the number of First-class marks and the number of fails fall within the expected range, which can slightly change the marks for parts of a question. If a paper's results still deviate significantly from expectations, scaling is applied, focused on the average, the fails and the Firsts. The department publishes the mark distribution and the effect of any scaling.

BANDS AND PASS MARKS
70+ First; 60-69 Upper Second; 50-59 Lower Second; 40-49 Third; below 40 fail at Levels 4-6 (pass mark 50 at Level 7). Marks of 30-39.99 at Levels 4-6 (40-49.99 at Level 7) are compensatable fails. Degree averages close to a higher boundary are reviewed by the Board of Examiners, with External Examiners looking at the scripts and projects of the candidates put forward. To remain on the MSci, students must show they can reach Upper Second standard; the Year Abroad route requires a 60% average over Years 1-2.

PROJECTS
The MSci project (PHYS70002, pass mark 50, must pass) is assessed as: literature review 15%, final report 50%, viva 15%, continuous assessment by the supervisor 10%, one-page summary and conference-style poster 10%. The report is marked by an assessor and the MSci project panel; the literature review and viva by supervisor and assessor.

WHEN MARKING A PRACTICE ANSWER
Award the indicative marks for each part of the question against its mark scheme, total and convert to a percentage, and report the class band; note that real papers may be moderated or scaled afterwards.

rubrics.title: CLCC / I-Explore and Horizons humanities and social sciences assessment expectations and level descriptors
rubrics.body:
CLCC does not publish a public band-by-band rubric for its Humanities and Social Sciences (HSS) modules; module lecturers issue the specific criteria. What it does publish is below: the class labels it uses, what markers look for, and level descriptors.

CLASS LABELS
Work is assessed against the assignment brief and the College's grading criteria and placed as excellent (First, 70+), very good (2:1, 60-69), good (2:2, 50-59) or adequate (Third, 40-49); below 40 fails. All credit-bearing written work is double marked, with a third marker if the two disagree, and marks are provisional until the external examiner and the June Board of Examiners confirm them.

WHAT MARKERS LOOK FOR IN HSS WRITING
- A critical argument: build a case, evaluate appropriate evidence, and explain why each point matters (critical means careful analysis, not negativity).
- Structure: an introduction stating the purpose and direction of the argument; body paragraphs that each make one distinct point; a conclusion that draws the argument together without new material.
- Style: precise, formal, readable prose using the module's terminology accurately, without cliches.
- Referencing: Harvard by default (or another agreed style used consistently); poor or inconsistent referencing loses marks.
- Length: keep to the word count or time limit; going significantly over or under reduces the mark (word counts include in-text citations, footnotes, tables and captions, not the bibliography).
- Following the brief and module-specific presentation instructions.

LEVEL DESCRIPTORS (expected standard rises with the student's level)
Level 4: knows the core principles, concepts and terms; describes, analyses and interprets defined aspects of a subject; communicates accurately for purpose and audience.
Level 5: critical understanding of principles and techniques; applies knowledge accurately to a range of problems and evaluates using established techniques; communicates arguments and ideas effectively.
Level 6: systematic, partly specialist knowledge informed by current thinking; handles abstract ideas and argues from competing perspectives; defines complex problems, chooses investigative strategies and evaluates their outcomes; communicates complex arguments effectively.
Level 7: deep, systematic understanding of a specialised field linked to other disciplines; works at a high level of abstraction; critically responds to existing theories and methods and proposes new concepts or approaches.
